title: Every Load Needs a Path to the Ground
summary: A structure is a set of paths that carry every load, from gravity, wind and earthquake, down to the foundation. Gravity systems hold the building up; lateral systems stop it swaying or overturning. The owner's decisions on grid, floor-to-floor height and mixed uses decide whether those paths are short and cheap or long and expensive.
body:
A structure is a set of paths that carry every load to the ground. When the path is straight and continuous, the building is cheap and calm. When the path has to bend, jump or transfer, the owner pays for every detour.

Recall

Q. Who is the authority having jurisdiction on a building project?

A. The official or body that interprets and enforces the code, usually the building official for construction and the fire marshal for fire systems; both may have a say.

Q. What is the difference between travel distance and common path of egress travel?

A. Travel distance is the length of the route from the most remote point to an exit. Common path is the part of that route before an occupant has a choice of two separate ways out.

Q. In concept, why does an owner-manager compare salary and dividends?

A. Because the two are taxed differently at the company and personal levels, and they affect things like retirement savings room differently. The rules depend on the jurisdiction; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, structure is usually the largest single trade in a mid-rise building's hard cost, and it sets the pace of construction: one floor at a time, floor after floor. It also sets limits nobody can change later: where columns stand, how high each floor is, where shafts can pass and how much load a roof can take. Most of those limits are fixed by decisions an owner makes in the first month: the unit mix, the parking arrangement and the uses stacked on top of each other.

Gravity and lateral

In plain English, a building has to do two things at once. It has to hold itself and its contents up, and it has to stand firm when wind pushes on it or the ground shakes. The first is the gravity system: slabs carry floor loads to beams, beams to columns or bearing walls, columns down to foundations. The second is the lateral force-resisting system: the elements that carry sideways loads down to the ground, such as concrete shear walls around stairs and elevators, steel braced frames or moment frames whose rigid joints resist sway.

The professional framing adds the word load path: the continuous chain of elements and connections that carries a given load from where it is applied to the foundation. Every load needs one. An engineer's first question about any scheme is whether each load path is continuous and as direct as possible. The loads themselves come from ASCE 7, the American Society of Civil Engineers' standard for minimum design loads, as adopted through the International Building Code (IBC): dead load, live load, roof and rain loads, wind and seismic loads, combined in defined ways. ASCE 7 also assigns each building a risk category, based on the consequence of failure, which raises the design loads for buildings that matter more. Verify the adopted edition with your engineer.

Worked example: the grid that does not line up

Take a hypothetical mixed-use building: parking at the base and apartments above. Parking wants columns spaced to fit cars and drive aisles, often around 30 feet apart in one direction, hypothetically. Apartments want walls and columns where bedrooms and corridors are, often on a different rhythm. If the apartment columns do not line up with the parking columns, each apartment column must stop on a deep beam or a thick slab that carries its load sideways to a column below. That is a transfer.

A transfer is not wrong. It is expensive and it concentrates risk. A transfer beam carrying several floors above it may be several feet deep, heavily reinforced and congested with steel, which slows construction and eats ceiling height. The alternative is to make the grids agree at concept stage: adjust the unit plan to the parking grid, or adjust the parking to the apartments. That is an owner's decision, because it trades unit layout, parking count and cost against each other.

Say that out loud now.

Every column that does not line up with the one below it is a beam I am paying to carry it sideways.

Worked example: floor-to-floor height

Floor-to-floor height is the distance from one floor surface to the next. It is made of the structure's depth, the ceiling space for ducts and pipes, and the room height you sell. Suppose a hypothetical residential floor has a 9-foot finished ceiling. A flat concrete slab with no beams might give a floor-to-floor of about 10 feet; a steel frame with beams and ducts below them might need 11 feet or more. Over many floors, that one foot adds to the building's height, to every square foot of exterior wall, to the length of every riser, and possibly to a zoning height limit that costs you a floor. Choosing the structural system is therefore a decision about the envelope and the zoning envelope as well as about structure.

Progressive collapse and peer review

Two ideas sit above the arithmetic. The first is robustness. Progressive collapse means the failure of one element triggers the failure of others, so a local event becomes a disproportionate collapse. Good structures have redundancy and continuity, ties that let loads find another path if one element is lost. Some codes and agencies have specific provisions for this in certain buildings; your engineer will say what applies [unverified — confirm independently].

The second is independent checking. A structural peer review is a review of the design by a separate qualified engineer. Some jurisdictions require it for tall or unusual buildings. Even where it is not required, an owner can commission one for a transfer level, an unusual connection or a new system. It is cheap relative to structure, and it puts a second set of eyes on the decisions that cannot be undone.

The construction view

Structure is also a schedule. A concrete frame is built in repeating floor cycles: formwork, reinforcement, embedded sleeves and conduits, pour, cure, strip and reshore. Anything that breaks the repetition, such as a transfer level, a change in column grid or a slab step, breaks the cycle and adds weeks. A steel frame moves faster on site but depends on shop drawings and fabrication long before erection. Either way, the structural system decision is a schedule decision, and Petra's critical path in Week 50 will have the structure on it from the first floor to the roof.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: structure is usually part of the building shell for depreciation or capital cost purposes, unlike some systems; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the engineer of record carries professional responsibility for the design, but an owner who alters scope or pushes changes without the engineer's review takes on risk. Banking: a lender's monitor will look hard at a transfer level or a new system because overruns cluster there. Governance: any change to structure after design approval goes through the engineer of record in writing. Estate: structural drawings and calculations are long-life records that should pass with the building. Exit: a buyer's engineer will ask for the drawings, calculations, peer review and special inspection reports.

Professional sign-off required: licensed structural engineer, as engineer of record; geotechnical engineer, for foundation loads and settlement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is fixing the architecture and the unit mix first and asking the structural engineer to make it stand up afterwards, which produces transfers, deep beams and lost ceiling height. The control is to bring the structural engineer in at concept, test two or three grid and system options against cost, height and schedule, and choose one before design development.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks of structure as the frame he sees on site. Most structural failures and many cost overruns start at connections and transfers, the places where a load changes direction. Ask where the loads change direction, and look there first.

Callback

In Week 100, Ivo taught that occupancy drives construction type and height and area limits. Structure answers to those choices: the construction type decides what the frame can be made of and how it must be protected from fire, which is Magnus's subject from last week. The fire rating, the code basis and the structural system are one decision seen from three seats.

Recap

Every load needs a continuous path to the ground. Gravity systems hold the building up and lateral systems resist wind and earthquake, with loads from ASCE 7 by risk category. Misaligned grids create transfers, floor-to-floor height drives envelope and zoning, and robustness and peer review protect the decisions you cannot undo.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse of 1981.
checklist: The structural engineer was engaged at concept stage.
I have compared two or three grid and system options on cost, height and schedule.
I know where every transfer is and why it exists.
I know the floor-to-floor height and what drives it.
I know the building's risk category and the adopted edition of ASCE 7.
I have decided whether to commission a structural peer review.
Every structural change after approval goes through the engineer of record in writing.
I know which floors break the construction cycle.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every load in a building needs a continuous path to the ground. The gravity system carries floors to beams, beams to columns or walls, and columns to foundations. The lateral system, such as shear walls or braced or moment frames, carries wind and earthquake loads down. ASCE 7, as adopted through the building code, sets the loads and a risk category that raises them for buildings that matter more. The owner's early choices decide whether the paths are straight or bent. If apartment columns do not line up with parking columns below, each one needs a transfer: a deep, expensive, slow beam. Floor-to-floor height comes from structure depth, ceiling space and room height, and it drives envelope area, riser lengths and zoning height. Good structures are robust, so one lost element cannot start a progressive collapse, and a peer review puts a second engineer on the decisions that cannot be undone.
terms: Load path — the continuous chain of elements and connections that carries a load from where it acts to the foundation.
Lateral force-resisting system — the walls, frames or braces that carry wind and earthquake loads to the ground.
Risk category — the classification in ASCE 7, based on the consequence of failure, that sets how conservative the design loads are.

hostile.q: Your scheme has a transfer level above the parking. Why should I believe your structural budget?
hostile.a: Because the transfer is priced as its own line, from the engineer's preliminary sizing, not hidden in a per-square-foot rate. We tested an aligned-grid option and chose the transfer knowingly because it gives a better unit plan, and the premium is in the pro forma. The transfer is also on our peer review scope and it has extra contingency until the shop drawings and reinforcement detailing are complete. I can show you the comparison.

title: The Hyatt Regency Walkways: One Rod Became Two
summary: On 17 July 1981, two suspended walkways in the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City collapsed during a crowded evening event, killing 114 people. A change in how the walkways hung, made between design and fabrication, doubled the load on a connection that was already weak. Seven forensic steps show how a load path was altered and nobody re-checked it.
body:
The Hyatt Regency walkways fell because a load path was changed and nobody owned the recheck. A connection that was already too weak was asked to carry twice its load, and a shop drawing review did not catch it.

Recall

Q. In reverse engineering a fire pump quote, how do you check pressure as well as volume?

A. Add the elevation loss, about 0.433 psi per foot of height, the pressure needed at the most remote sprinkler and the friction loss, then compare the total with what the pump and supply can deliver.

Q. Why is a corridor dead end a problem in egress design?

A. Because an occupant who walks into a dead end must turn back toward the fire to escape, so codes limit dead-end length.

Q. In concept, why can retirement savings room depend on how an owner pays himself?

A. Because in some systems the room to contribute to certain retirement accounts is tied to earned income such as salary, not to dividends. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the case structural engineers teach first, and for an owner it is the most important one in the curriculum. Nothing about it was exotic: a common building type, an ordinary connection, a reasonable request from a fabricator to make installation easier. It killed 114 people because the change moved through the design and approval process without anyone checking what it did to the load path. You will approve changes like it on every project.

The facts below are from the public record, including the investigation by the National Bureau of Standards, now the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Where I describe motives, that is interpretation.

1. Timeline

The Hyatt Regency Kansas City opened in 1980 with a large atrium crossed by suspended walkways. The second-floor walkway hung directly below the fourth-floor walkway, and a third-floor walkway was offset to one side. During construction, in 1979, part of the atrium roof collapsed; a review followed, and it did not reach the walkway connections. On the evening of 17 July 1981, during a crowded event in the atrium, the fourth-floor walkway's hanger connections failed. It fell onto the second-floor walkway, and both fell to the atrium floor. One hundred and fourteen people died and more than two hundred were injured.

2. Key decisions

The original design hung both walkways from continuous rods running from the atrium ceiling, through the fourth-floor walkway, down to the second-floor walkway. During detailing and fabrication, the arrangement was changed to two sets of rods: one set from the ceiling to the fourth-floor walkway, and a second set from the fourth-floor walkway down to the second. The shop drawings showing the change were reviewed and stamped. That single change meant the fourth-floor connection now carried the second-floor walkway as well as its own.

3. Assumptions

The fabricator appears to have assumed the change was a practical detail, since a single continuous rod is awkward to install. The engineers appear to have assumed the shop drawing review was a check on conformance, not a fresh design check of the altered connection. And the investigation found that the original connection, before any change, did not meet the capacity the building code required. Everyone assumed someone else had checked the connection.

4. Incentives

Fabricators are paid to fabricate and erect efficiently, and a simpler rod arrangement saves time and money. Engineers under fee and schedule pressure review large volumes of shop drawings quickly. Owners want the building open. None of those incentives rewards the slow question: what does this change do to the forces in the connection?

Say that out loud now.

A change that makes installation easier can change where the load goes. Every such change gets a load path check, in writing.

5. Warning signs ignored

The atrium roof collapse during construction was a signal that the atrium's structure deserved a thorough review; the review that followed did not examine the walkway hangers. Reports from the period also describe people noticing the walkways move under load. A structure that visibly moves or a related failure during construction is a reason to stop and check the whole system, not only the part that failed.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return for the structure was the approval of the double-rod shop drawings without a recalculation, because from then on the connection was built to fail under a heavy crowd. Every day afterwards, the building was waiting for a load large enough to find the weakness.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a break in responsibility for the load path. The connection design was not fully calculated at the outset, a change to it was proposed by one party and approved by another, and neither treated the approval as a structural recalculation. The box beam connection failed where the rod nut pulled through it, which is exactly where the doubled load concentrated.

What followed

The engineers of record lost their licences in Missouri after disciplinary proceedings, and the case is now central to engineering ethics teaching. The profession's practice on shop drawings and delegated connection design was tightened and clarified: who designs a connection, who checks it, and what a review stamp does and does not mean. For an owner, the lasting change is that the responsibility for each connection should be written down before fabrication begins.

The owner's controls today

Three controls follow directly. First, the construction contract and the structural specifications should state who designs each connection: the engineer of record, or a delegated engineer working for the fabricator, who then seals the calculations. Second, any substitution or change to a structural element or connection after the design is issued should require the engineer of record's written confirmation that the load path and capacity still work, separate from routine shop drawing review. Third, on a building with unusual elements, such as suspended walkways, long transfers or cantilevers, commission an independent peer review of those elements before fabrication. None of these is expensive compared with the structure. Each would have interrupted the chain that led to the collapse.

Where the same pattern hides on your projects

The Hyatt pattern is not limited to walkways. It appears wherever a load path runs through a detail that a fabricator or installer has reason to change: hangers for heavy mechanical equipment, balcony connections, canopy supports, stair stringers, precast panel connections and the anchors for rooftop units. Each is small relative to the frame, often delegated, and easy to alter during installation. On a hypothetical residential building, list every hung, cantilevered or delegated element at the start of construction, and treat that list as the place your Rule 103 discipline is applied first.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structural change that travels through the shop drawing process looking like a detail. The control is a contract and specification that require any change to a structural member or connection to be submitted as a change, with sealed calculations, and confirmed in writing by the engineer of record before fabrication, separate from routine review.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that a stamped shop drawing means the structure has been checked. A review stamp usually says the submission conforms generally to the design intent. Ask your engineer what their stamp means, and who has calculated each connection.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX taught that the order of precedence in a contract decides which document wins when two conflict. Shop drawings are where that question becomes physical. If the specification says the engineer designs connections and the shop drawing shows a different connection, the contract must say which governs and who checks the difference.

Recap

Two walkways in the Hyatt Regency Kansas City fell in 1981, killing 114 people. A change from continuous rods to two sets of rods doubled the load on a connection that was already under capacity, and the shop drawing approval did not recalculate it. The root cause was a break in responsibility for the load path.

Rule 103: Never let a structural member or connection change after design without the engineer of record confirming in writing that the whole load path still works; a shop drawing stamp is not that confirmation.

Next: Sage on The Money: what grid, floor-to-floor and transfers do to cost, units and value.
checklist: My contract states who designs each structural connection.
Delegated connection design comes with sealed calculations.
Any structural substitution is submitted as a change, not a shop drawing detail.
The engineer of record confirms in writing that the load path still works.
I know what my engineer's shop drawing stamp means.
Unusual elements such as suspended walkways or long cantilevers get peer review.
A failure or unexpected movement during construction triggers a whole-system review.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 17 July 1981, two suspended walkways in the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City collapsed during a crowded evening event, and 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from continuous rods. During detailing and fabrication, that was changed to two sets of rods, so the fourth-floor connection had to carry the second-floor walkway as well as its own. The investigation found the original connection was already short of the code's required capacity. The change was approved on the shop drawings without a fresh calculation. The root cause was a break in responsibility for the load path: one party proposed a change, another approved it, and nobody recalculated it. The engineers lost their licences. Rule 103: never let a structural member or connection change after design without the engineer of record confirming in writing that the whole load path still works. A shop drawing stamp is not that confirmation.
terms: Shop drawing — a fabricator's or subcontractor's detailed drawing of how an element will be made and installed, submitted for review against the design.
Delegated design — a design responsibility, such as connection design, assigned by contract to a specialty engineer who seals the calculations.
Connection — the joint where structural members meet and transfer load, often the most critical point in a load path.

hostile.q: Your steel fabricator wants to change the cantilever connections to speed erection. Your engineer stamped the shop drawings. Are we safe?
hostile.a: Not on the stamp alone. A shop drawing stamp checks general conformance, not a new design. I have required the fabricator's delegated engineer to submit sealed calculations for the revised connection, and the engineer of record to confirm in writing that the load path and capacity still work. Fabrication of those connections waits for that letter. I will send you a copy, and the cantilever is also on our peer review scope.

rule: Rule 103: Never let a structural member or connection change after design without the engineer of record confirming in writing that the whole load path still works; a shop drawing stamp is not that confirmation.

title: What Grid, Floor Height and Transfers Do to Cost and Value
summary: Structural decisions move cost in three places at once: the frame itself, the envelope and services that grow with height, and the units or parking gained or lost. A transfer level and an extra foot of floor-to-floor are priced in dollars and in schedule. Put them in the pro forma before you fall in love with a plan.
body:
The structural frame is only the first cost of a structural decision. The second is everything that grows with height, and the third is the rentable area and parking you gain or lose. Price all three before you choose a plan.

Recall

Q. In the fire marshal meeting, what do you never argue as the reason for an alternate?

A. Cost. The reason is equivalent safety, supported by evidence; the cost saving is the owner's own business.

Q. What is an accessible route?

A. A continuous unobstructed path that a person using a wheelchair can travel, connecting accessible spaces and elements in and around a building.

Q. In concept, what is integration in owner-manager taxation?

A. The idea that income earned through a company and paid out to the owner should bear roughly the same total tax as income earned directly. Whether a system achieves it depends on its rules; verify that against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, structure is often the largest trade on a mid-rise job, and the decisions that set its cost are made before most owners think of structure at all. Once the unit mix, parking layout and ground-floor uses are fixed, the structural engineer can only make the plan stand up. This lesson shows how to put the structural choices into the numbers you already track: total development cost, net operating income (NOI), yield on cost and schedule.

Three places the money moves

In plain English: when you pick a structural system or a grid, you change what the frame costs, you change how tall the building is, which changes the cost of everything wrapped around it, and you change how many units or parking spaces fit. The professional framing calls the second effect a height multiplier: costs that scale with height and with exterior wall area, such as curtain wall or cladding, risers, elevator travel and scaffolding time. The third effect is efficiency: rentable or saleable area divided by gross area.

Worked example: one foot of floor-to-floor

Hypothetical round numbers. A residential building has ten floors above a podium, each 10,000 square feet in plan, with a perimeter of 400 feet. Option A, a flat concrete slab, gives a floor-to-floor of 10 feet. Option B, a framed scheme with deeper beams, needs 11 feet to keep the same ceiling height.

The extra foot on each floor adds 10 feet of height overall. Exterior wall area rises by 400 feet of perimeter times 10 feet, which is 4,000 square feet. At a hypothetical 80 dollars per square foot for the wall system, that is 320,000 dollars. Add risers, stair and elevator travel and a longer facade schedule, say another 150,000 dollars in total. Option B costs about 470,000 dollars more around the frame before you compare the frames themselves. If Option B's frame is 300,000 dollars cheaper, the true difference is a 170,000 dollar penalty, not a saving.

If the zoning envelope caps height, the extra 10 feet may cost a whole floor of apartments. At a hypothetical 8,500 rentable square feet and 30 dollars per square foot a year, that floor earns 255,000 dollars of NOI, worth about 4,250,000 dollars at a 6 percent cap rate. A cheaper frame that loses a floor is the most expensive option on the table.

Say that out loud now.

I compare structural systems on the whole building, not on the frame alone.

Worked example: the transfer premium

Now take the misaligned grid from Day 1. The apartment columns do not line up with the parking below, so a transfer level carries them. Hypothetically, the transfer adds 900,000 dollars of concrete and reinforcement, three extra weeks on the frame schedule, and 18 inches of depth that the parking level loses or the building gains.

Price the schedule. If the construction loan averages 18,000,000 dollars during the frame stage at 7 percent a year, three weeks of interest is about 18,000,000 times 0.07 times 3 divided by 52, or about 73,000 dollars. Add general conditions, the contractor's site overhead, at a hypothetical 60,000 dollars a week, which is 180,000 dollars. The transfer's true premium is about 1,150,000 dollars.

Against that, test the aligned-grid option. Aligning the apartments with the parking grid might lose two units a floor through awkward layouts, or force a less efficient parking layout that loses stalls. If two units a floor across ten floors each earn 18,000 dollars of NOI a year, that is 360,000 dollars of NOI, worth 6,000,000 dollars at a 6 percent cap rate. On those numbers, the transfer is worth paying for. On other numbers, it is not. The point is that both options go into the pro forma.

Yield on cost

Bring it together. Suppose the base scheme costs 40,000,000 dollars and earns 2,400,000 dollars of NOI, a 6.0 percent yield on cost. Adding the 1,150,000 dollar transfer and keeping the 360,000 dollars of NOI it protects gives a cost of 41,150,000 dollars against NOI of 2,400,000 dollars. Compared with the aligned option, which saves the transfer but earns 2,040,000 dollars on 40,000,000 dollars, a yield on cost of 5.1 percent, the transfer scheme yields about 5.83 percent. The transfer wins by about 73 basis points.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: structural quality is the longest-lived part of the asset. Cladding, finishes and systems are replaced; the frame usually is not. A building with a robust, well-documented structure holds value through cycles and is easier to refinance, because a lender's engineer can reach a clean conclusion quickly. Keep the drawings, calculations, special inspection reports and peer review as part of the asset's title file.

Worked example: the parking efficiency trade

Structure also decides how many cars fit. Hypothetically, a parking level with a 30-foot column grid in one direction might park cars at about 350 square feet per stall including aisles, while a grid with columns intruding into drive aisles or stall ends might need closer to 400 square feet per stall. On a 30,000 square foot parking level, that is about 86 stalls against 75, a loss of 11. If each stall is worth a hypothetical 1,200 dollars a year of parking income or supports units the zoning would otherwise not allow, the grid choice moves either income or entitlement, not only concrete.

A lender reading your pro forma will ask the same thing from the other side: which structural assumption, if wrong, moves the yield most? Run each option at plus and minus 10 percent on its frame cost and on its schedule, and show which survives the downside. An option that wins only on the base case is a bet, not a choice, and the options study should say so plainly.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a structural system on frame cost per square foot alone, while the height multiplier and the efficiency effect move several times as much money. The control is a structural options study at concept stage that prices each option on total development cost, schedule and NOI, and feeds the result into the pro forma.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner accepts the first plan the architect draws and then asks the engineer to make it cheaper. By then, the expensive decisions are fixed. Ask for the structural options before the plan is final.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught yield on cost and the development spread: the gap between what a project yields on its cost and the cap rate the market pays. Every structural decision moves both sides of that ratio at once, which is why an engineer's choice of slab can widen or close the spread that makes the whole project worth doing.

Recap

Structural decisions move money in three places: the frame, everything that grows with height, and the units or parking you gain or lose. One foot of floor-to-floor can cost more than a cheaper frame saves, and a transfer can be worth paying for if it protects income. Price every option on the whole building.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: how the code governs structure, and how Canada and Guyana approach it.
checklist: I have a structural options study priced on total development cost.
I know the height multiplier: what grows with every foot of height.
I know whether the zoning height limit binds.
I price a transfer in materials, schedule, interest and general conditions.
I compare each option's NOI as well as its cost.
I calculate yield on cost for each structural option.
I keep the structural records with the asset's title file.
head: Field checklist
speak: A structural decision moves money in three places. First, the frame itself. Second, everything that grows with height: exterior wall, risers, elevator travel and facade schedule. Third, efficiency: the units and parking you gain or lose. In a hypothetical case, one extra foot of floor-to-floor on ten floors added about 470,000 dollars around the frame, more than a cheaper frame saved, and could cost a whole floor if zoning caps the height. A transfer level is priced in concrete and steel, plus weeks of interest and general conditions; in the example about 1,150,000 dollars. But if aligning the grid would lose income worth 6,000,000 dollars of value, the transfer is worth paying for. So I study structural options at concept stage and price each on total cost, schedule, NOI and yield on cost, never on frame cost per square foot alone.
terms: Floor-to-floor height — the vertical distance from one floor surface to the next, made of structural depth, service space and finished ceiling height.
Height multiplier — the costs that rise with building height, such as exterior wall area, risers and elevator travel.
Efficiency ratio — rentable or saleable area divided by gross floor area.

hostile.q: Your contractor priced a steel frame cheaper than concrete. Why are you choosing concrete?
hostile.a: Because the steel frame needs about a foot more floor-to-floor to keep our ceiling height, which adds exterior wall, risers and schedule that more than consume its frame saving, and it pushes us against the zoning height limit. I have the options study that prices both schemes on total cost and NOI. On the whole building, concrete is cheaper and keeps every floor of income.

title: How the Code Governs Structure: Loads, Materials, Inspections and Review
summary: The building code adopts ASCE 7 for loads and material standards such as ACI 318 and AISC 360 for design, then requires special inspections and, in some places, peer review. The engineer of record seals the design; the owner contracts the inspections. Canada and Guyana approach the same questions through different systems.
body:
The building code does not design a structure. It points to load and material standards, says who must seal the design, and requires inspections that prove the building matches it. An owner's duties sit in the inspection chapter more than in the design chapters.

Recall

Q. What does a structural peer review add to a project?

A. An independent check of the design by a separate qualified engineer, focused on the decisions that cannot be undone, such as transfers and unusual connections.

Q. What is a fire watch?

A. Trained people patrolling a building to detect fire while a protection system is impaired.

Q. In concept, why should an owner understand how retirement income is drawn?

A. Because the order and form of withdrawals from different accounts can change the total tax paid over a lifetime. Verify the rules against the primary source, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when something goes wrong with a structure, the first question in any dispute is which standard applied and who was responsible for meeting it. You do not need to read ACI 318. You do need to know the chain of documents and duties, so you can see whether your contracts and your project team cover every link. This lesson teaches the structure of the rules, not a design.

The chain of documents

In the United States, the International Building Code (IBC), as adopted and amended by the jurisdiction, contains the structural design chapter. That chapter adopts ASCE 7 for minimum design loads: dead, live, snow, rain, wind, flood and seismic, and the combinations in which they are checked. Material chapters then point to the design standards: ACI 318 for structural concrete, AISC 360 for structural steel, with AISC 341 for steel seismic systems where seismic design requires it, and other standards for masonry, wood and cold-formed steel. Each is cited in a particular edition. Verify against the current adopted edition before relying on any provision.

The design must be prepared and sealed by a licensed engineer under the state's licensing law. That engineer, the engineer of record, takes professional responsibility for the structural design, though parts of it, such as connections or precast elements, may be delegated to specialty engineers who seal their own work.

Special inspections and structural observation

The code's special inspection chapter requires certain work to be inspected by qualified special inspectors, beyond the building department's routine inspections: reinforcement placement, concrete placement and testing, high-strength bolting, structural welding, and others depending on the project. A statement of special inspections, prepared by the design professional and submitted with the permit, lists what will be inspected, how often and by whom. In many cases the owner, not the contractor, must engage the special inspection agency, to keep the inspector independent of the party being inspected [unverified — confirm independently]. Structural observation, which is a visit by the engineer to see that construction generally conforms, may also be required for certain buildings.

Worked example: the inspector the contractor hired

Hypothetically, a contractor offers to include special inspections in its lump sum "to keep things simple". The owner accepts. Months later, a concrete strength problem arises, and the inspection reports were issued by a firm paid by the party whose work was in question. Even if the reports are honest, their independence is now arguable, and the building official may question them. The control is to engage the special inspection agency directly, as the owner, at the start, and to have its reports sent to the owner, the engineer of record and the building official at the same time.

Say that out loud now.

I hire the special inspector myself, and the reports go to me, my engineer and the building official at once.

Robustness and peer review in the rules

The IBC contains structural integrity provisions for certain high-rise buildings, requiring ties and continuity so a building can resist disproportionate collapse [unverified — confirm independently]. Federal agencies have their own progressive collapse criteria for buildings they own. Some jurisdictions require independent structural peer review for tall or unusual buildings or for performance-based seismic designs. Where peer review is not required, the owner can still commission one, and the contract should say whether the engineer of record must respond to its comments.

Two Systems

This is an odd week from Week 19 on, so here is a conceptual comparison; verify against primary source before you rely on any of it. In Canada, the National Building Code of Canada is a model code that provinces and territories adopt, sometimes with changes, as their own building codes. Its structural design part sets loads and refers to Canadian Standards Association (CSA) design standards, such as CSA A23.3 for concrete and CSA S16 for steel. Licensing of engineers is provincial, and the rules on sealing, field review and who engages inspection vary by province.

In Guyana, building approval and the standards applied are set by national legislation and administered through national and local authorities, and the country's standards body has a role in adopting technical standards. Regional work in the Caribbean has produced building code frameworks drawn in part from international model codes. What is legally required on a given project, which edition is adopted, and who must review and inspect, is a question for a Guyanese professional and the approving authority; verify against primary source. The practical point is that the same physical questions, loads, materials, sealing and inspection, are answered by different documents, and a project crossing borders must name the governing set in writing on day one.

Worked example: the change of edition

Hypothetically, a project is permitted under one edition of the code, and the jurisdiction adopts a newer edition before a later phase is permitted. The newer edition may cite a newer ASCE 7, with different wind or seismic provisions. Phase two, designed by copying phase one's drawings, could then be designed to the wrong loads. The control is to confirm the governing edition for each permit, in writing, and to ask the engineer of record what changed between editions before reusing any design.

For an owner, the practical output of this chapter is a short list kept in the project file: the adopted editions, the engineer of record and each delegated engineer, the special inspection agency and its contract, whether structural observation and peer review apply, and the date each was confirmed. When a lender's monitor, an insurer or a buyer's engineer asks how the structure was governed, that page answers in one minute.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a gap in the chain: a delegated element with no sealed calculation, a special inspection nobody engaged, or an edition nobody named. The control is a structural responsibility matrix at the start of construction listing every element, its designer, its sealing engineer, its inspector and the standard and edition that governs it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the building department's inspections are the quality control. They are a regulatory check, often brief. Special inspections, structural observation and the owner's own quality plan are what actually find problems.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX with Vera taught that an engagement letter should state scope, instructions and deliverables precisely, because what is not in the scope is not owed. The statement of special inspections and the structural responsibility matrix are engagement letters for the structure. If an element is not on them, nobody has agreed to check it.

Recap

The code adopts ASCE 7 for loads and ACI, AISC and other standards for materials, in named editions. A licensed engineer of record seals the design, specialty engineers seal delegated parts, and special inspectors, engaged independently, verify the work. Canada and Guyana answer the same questions through different documents, so name the governing set on day one.

Professional sign-off required: licensed structural engineer of record; licensed delegated engineers for any delegated design; special inspection agency.

Next: Bram on The Numbers: a gravity load takedown and what a transfer has to carry.
checklist: I know the adopted edition of the IBC, ASCE 7, ACI 318 and AISC 360 for my project.
Every delegated element has a named sealing engineer.
I have read the statement of special inspections.
I engage the special inspection agency directly as owner.
Inspection reports go to me, the engineer and the building official at once.
I know whether structural observation or peer review is required.
I have a structural responsibility matrix for every element.
On a cross-border project, the governing codes are named in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: The building code, as adopted, does not design a structure. It adopts ASCE 7 for loads and material standards, such as ACI 318 for concrete and AISC 360 for steel, each in a named edition. A licensed engineer of record seals the design, and specialty engineers seal any delegated parts, such as connections or precast. The special inspection chapter requires independent special inspectors for critical work like reinforcement, concrete, bolting and welding, listed in a statement of special inspections; I engage that agency myself, and the reports go to me, my engineer and the building official at the same time. Some buildings need structural observation, structural integrity ties or peer review. In Canada, the provinces adopt the National Building Code and CSA standards; in Guyana, national law and authorities set what applies; I verify against the primary source. On any project, I keep a responsibility matrix for every element.
terms: Engineer of record — the licensed engineer who seals the structural design and takes professional responsibility for it.
Special inspection — inspection of critical structural work by a qualified independent inspector, required by the building code in addition to routine inspections.
Statement of special inspections — the document, submitted with the permit, listing what will be specially inspected, how often and by whom.

hostile.q: Your contractor's lump sum includes special inspections. Why should I trust the inspection reports?
hostile.a: You should not have to, and that is why I am changing it. I have engaged the special inspection agency directly as owner, under a separate contract, and its reports go to me, the engineer of record and the building official at the same time. The contractor's lump sum will be reduced by the inspection allowance. I can send you the agency's scope and the statement of special inspections.

title: A Gravity Load Takedown, and What a Transfer Has to Carry
summary: A load takedown adds up, floor by floor, the weight each column carries to the foundation, using tributary area, dead and live loads and a code load combination. Run it on one hypothetical column and you see why a transfer beam becomes so large, and why a roof tank or a change of use above can overload a structure designed for something else.
body:
A load takedown is simple arithmetic done patiently: area times load, floor by floor, down to the foundation. Do it once on a hypothetical column and you will understand transfers, heavy roofs and changes of use better than any diagram can teach you.

Recall

Q. Who should engage the special inspection agency, and why?

A. Usually the owner, so the inspector is independent of the contractor whose work is being inspected; confirm the local requirement.

Q. What is an area of refuge?

A. A protected space where people who cannot use stairs can wait for assistance during an emergency, with communication to the building's emergency staff.

Q. In concept, what is the difference between a tax deduction and a tax credit?

A. A deduction reduces the income that is taxed; a credit reduces the tax itself. Their value and availability depend on the system; verify that against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will not size columns. But you will be asked to approve things that add load: a rooftop water tank, a green roof, a change from offices to a gym, heavy mechanical units. Each one is a load takedown question. If you can do the arithmetic in rough form, you will know when to stop and call the engineer. Every number below is a hypothetical round figure chosen to teach the method. The real loads and combinations come from the adopted edition of ASCE 7 and the engineer of record.

Step 1: tributary area

Plain English: each column carries the floor around it, out to roughly halfway to the next column in each direction. That patch is its tributary area. For an interior column on a regular grid with columns 30 feet apart both ways, the tributary area is 30 feet times 30 feet, which equals 900 square feet per floor.

Step 2: the loads on each square foot

Dead load is the permanent weight: the structure itself and fixed finishes. A hypothetical 8-inch concrete slab weighs about 100 pounds per square foot (psf), because normal-weight reinforced concrete weighs about 150 pounds per cubic foot and 8 inches is two thirds of a foot. Add a hypothetical 20 psf for partitions, ceilings, floor finishes and services. Dead load is 120 psf.

Live load is the movable weight: people and furniture. ASCE 7 gives minimum values by use; a commonly cited value for residential rooms is 40 psf, with higher values for corridors, assembly areas and parking [unverified — confirm independently]. Use 40 psf here.

Step 3: load per floor

Dead load per floor is 900 square feet times 120 psf, which equals 108,000 pounds, or 108 kips, since a kip is 1,000 pounds. Live load per floor is 900 times 40, which equals 36,000 pounds, or 36 kips.

Step 4: the load combination

Design does not simply add dead and live load. It multiplies each by a load factor and checks several combinations, taking the worst. Two of the basic strength combinations in ASCE 7 are 1.4 times dead load, and 1.2 times dead load plus 1.6 times live load [unverified — confirm independently]. For one floor: 1.4 times 108 equals 151.2 kips. And 1.2 times 108 plus 1.6 times 36 equals 129.6 plus 57.6, which is 187.2 kips. The second governs, at 187.2 kips per floor.

Say that out loud now.

Tributary area times load, factored, floor by floor. That is the whole method.

Step 5: add up the floors

Suppose this hypothetical column carries the roof and four floors, five levels in all, and, for simplicity, each level is loaded the same. Five times 187.2 equals 936 kips of factored load at the base of the column. In real design, live load reduction often lowers the live part for columns carrying large areas, so this figure is conservative. Add the column's own weight and the engineer has the load the foundation must take.

Step 6: what a transfer has to carry

Now stop this column at a transfer level. Its 936 kips must be carried sideways by a beam to two columns below, 30 feet apart, with the transferred column landing at midspan. For a simply supported beam with a point load at midspan, the maximum bending moment is the load times the span divided by 4. That is 936 times 30 divided by 4, which equals 7,020 kip-feet. For comparison, a typical floor beam in a building like this might carry a few hundred kip-feet. The transfer beam must be many times stronger, which is why it is so deep, so heavily reinforced and so slow to build. In practice the beam is often continuous over several supports, which changes the numbers, but not the lesson.

Step 7: the tank on the roof

Last week, Magnus showed a quoted fire water tank of 120,000 gallons. Water weighs about 8.34 pounds per gallon, so that tank, full, weighs about 1,000,000 pounds, or 1,000 kips. If it sits on a roof designed for a normal roof load, it is a different building. Even a 36,000 gallon tank is about 300 kips. Spread over a 900 square foot bay, 300 kips is about 333 psf, far above an ordinary roof design load. This is why every heavy item needs to be in the structural design from the start, and why a change of use or a new rooftop unit always goes to the engineer.

Step 8: check the units every time

Most arithmetic mistakes in a takedown are unit mistakes: pounds against kips, square feet against square metres, a slab thickness entered in inches where feet were meant. A quick discipline is to write the unit beside every number, as above, and to estimate the answer in your head before you calculate it. Nine hundred square feet at roughly 160 pounds of total load is about 144 kips unfactored; if your calculator says 14 or 1,400, something has slipped.

Worked example in metric, for a cross-border project

The same method works in metric. Hypothetically, a column on a 9 metre by 9 metre grid carries 81 square metres per floor. A dead load of 5.75 kilonewtons per square metre gives about 466 kilonewtons, and a live load of 1.9 kilonewtons per square metre gives about 154 kilonewtons. With the same factors, 1.2 times 466 plus 1.6 times 154 is about 559 plus 246, or 805 kilonewtons per floor. The numbers are different because the units are different; the arithmetic is identical. Never mix the two systems in one calculation, and on a project that crosses a border, agree at the start which system the drawings use.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is adding load after design, a tank, a planter, a heavy fit-out or a change of use, without anyone running the takedown again. The control is a rule that every added weight above a stated threshold, and every change of use, goes to the engineer of record for written confirmation before it is ordered.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a strong-looking slab can take anything. Slabs are designed to a stated load, often printed on the structural drawings. Read the design loads note on the general notes sheet, and keep it with the building's operating manual.

Callback

In Week 11, Nadia taught that units and time periods must match before any calculation means anything: a monthly cost against an annual income produces nonsense. Structural arithmetic is the same discipline in pounds and kips. Write the unit beside every number and most mistakes become visible.

Recap

Tributary area 900 square feet; dead load 120 psf and live load 40 psf give 108 and 36 kips a floor; the governing combination gives 187.2 kips a floor and 936 kips over five levels. A transfer carrying that load at midspan of 30 feet faces 7,020 kip-feet of moment. A full fire tank can weigh 1,000 kips. Every added load goes to the engineer.

Professional sign-off required: licensed structural engineer of record, for loads, combinations and member design.

Next: Bram in The Room: the peer review meeting when the contractor wants to change the transfer.
checklist: I can estimate a column's tributary area.
I know the design dead and live loads on the structural general notes.
I know the governing load combination is chosen by the engineer from ASCE 7.
I check units on every number.
Every added weight above a set threshold goes to the engineer of record.
Every change of use triggers a structural check.
Rooftop tanks and heavy equipment are in the structural design from the start.
head: Field checklist
speak: A load takedown is area times load, factored, floor by floor. In a hypothetical case, an interior column on a 30-foot grid carries 900 square feet per floor. Dead load of 120 pounds per square foot gives 108 kips; live load of 40 gives 36 kips. The governing combination, 1.2 times dead plus 1.6 times live, gives 187.2 kips a floor, and over five levels 936 kips, before any live load reduction. If that column stops on a transfer beam at midspan of a 30-foot span, the moment is load times span over four, about 7,020 kip-feet, many times an ordinary floor beam. And a full 120,000 gallon fire tank weighs about 1,000 kips. That is why every added weight and every change of use goes to the engineer of record before it is ordered. The real loads and combinations come from the adopted edition of ASCE 7.
terms: Tributary area — the patch of floor whose load a column or beam carries, usually out to halfway to the next support.
Kip — a unit of force equal to 1,000 pounds, used in structural calculations.
Load combination — a set of factored loads, such as 1.2 dead plus 1.6 live, checked together to find the governing design case.

hostile.q: The new tenant wants a gym with free weights on the third floor. The building was designed for apartments. Can we sign the lease?
hostile.a: Not until the engineer of record has checked it. A gym, especially with heavy weights and drop zones, can carry much higher live loads and impact than residential use. I have asked the engineer to run the takedown for that bay with the tenant's equipment plan, and to say whether the floor works as is, needs local strengthening or limits on equipment. The lease will carry a load limit clause either way.

title: The Peer Review Meeting When the Contractor Wants to Change the Transfer
summary: A meeting with the engineer of record, the peer reviewer and the contractor, who proposes a cheaper, faster transfer detail. The scene gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the contractor's question and when to stay silent. The goal is a decision made on the load path, in writing, not in the room.
body:
When a contractor offers to save money on a transfer, the owner's job is not to say yes or no in the room. It is to make sure the load path is checked by the right people, in writing, before anything is fabricated.

Recall

Q. What is the governing load combination in a simple gravity takedown?

A. Commonly 1.2 times dead load plus 1.6 times live load, compared against 1.4 times dead load, with the larger governing; the engineer confirms from the adopted ASCE 7.

Q. What did the Hyatt Regency shop drawing change do to the load path?

A. It made the fourth-floor connection carry the second-floor walkway as well as its own, doubling the load on a connection that was already under capacity.

Q. In concept, why should personal tax planning be coordinated with company decisions?

A. Because how money leaves a company, and when, changes the personal tax paid, so the two cannot be decided separately. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, value-engineering offers arrive when the job is late or over budget, and they arrive with a saving and a schedule gain attached. On a transfer level, a change can be harmless or it can be the Hyatt Regency in a new form. You will not be able to judge the engineering. You can judge whether the process protects the load path.

The scene

A hypothetical mixed-use building is at the transfer level above the parking. The contractor proposes replacing the cast-in-place transfer beams with a precast and post-tensioned scheme designed by its specialty engineer. It claims a saving of 400,000 dollars and two weeks. Present are the engineer of record, the independent peer reviewer you commissioned, the contractor's project manager and its specialty engineer, your owner's representative and you.

The opening

You open: "Thank you for the proposal. The saving matters to us, and so does the schedule. Before we decide anything, we need three things: the engineer of record's view of whether the load path and the connections to the columns above and below still work, the peer reviewer's view of the same, and the effect on everything else the transfer touches, such as the slab, the services through it and the fire rating. We will decide in writing after that."

Then stop. You have set the decision rule. Everyone now knows the answer will not be given in the meeting.

Say that out loud now.

We will decide in writing, after the engineer of record and the peer reviewer have checked the load path.

The question behind the question

The contractor's project manager asks: "Can we at least release the precast order today so we don't lose the slot?" On the surface, that is about a manufacturing slot. The question behind it is whether you will let commitment run ahead of approval. Once precast is ordered, the cost of saying no rises every day, and the pressure to accept moves from the contractor to you.

The line to say: "No order until the engineer of record confirms in writing. If the slot matters, tell me the latest date we can confirm without losing it, and I will ask the engineers whether they can respond by then. If they cannot, we keep the original design." That turns a pressure tactic into a date.

Lines never to say

Never say "if it's cheaper and the engineers don't object, go ahead". Silence from an engineer is not approval. Never say "your guy's stamp is good enough". The contractor's specialty engineer seals his part, but the engineer of record must confirm it works with the rest of the structure. Never take sides in a technical disagreement between the engineer of record and the peer reviewer in the room. If they disagree, your line is: "Please put your positions in writing and meet to resolve them. I will decide when you have."

When to stay silent

When the engineer of record says, "I need to look at the connection into the columns above," do not fill the pause. That sentence is the most valuable thing said in the meeting. Write it down and let it stand.

How the best do it

Owners and contractors with strong records on complex buildings commonly run every structural substitution through a formal change process: a written proposal, the specialty engineer's sealed calculations, the engineer of record's written response, the peer reviewer's comments where one is engaged, and an owner decision recorded in the decision log, before procurement. A small developer can copy this with a single form and a rule that no substitution is ordered without the engineer of record's signature on it.

Time and energy on a rotating shift

This month's thread is energy. A meeting like this one often lands after a night shift, when judgment is weakest and the temptation to agree and leave is strongest. If you can, schedule structural decisions for your best hours, not your worst. If you cannot, say less: open with the decision rule, write everything down, and decide later in writing, which is the right process anyway.

Your shift pattern can also be an advantage. Grid control rooms taught you to defer a switching decision until the study is complete rather than act on a confident voice. Treat a value-engineering offer the same way: no switching until the study is in.

A second voice in the room: the peer reviewer

The peer reviewer says: "I would want to see the deflection of the new beams under the floors above, because partitions and finishes up there were detailed for a stiffer transfer." That is a question that would cost money to answer, and the contractor's project manager may sigh. Your line: "Thank you. Please put that in your written comments, and we will ask the specialty engineer to address it." Do not judge whether the concern is large or small. Your job is to make sure every concern is answered in writing before the decision.

After the meeting, send a one-page note within 24 hours: the proposal, the questions each engineer raised, who owes each answer and by when, and the rule that no procurement is released until the engineer of record confirms in writing. Copy the contractor. That note is the record that the decision process existed, which matters if anyone asks later why a cheaper scheme was or was not adopted.

One last discipline. If the review confirms the substitution works, accept it gracefully and share the saving as the contract provides. A contractor who learns that good proposals are checked fairly and adopted will bring you more of them. A contractor who learns that every proposal is refused will stop offering, and you lose the value engineering that genuinely helps.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a substitution accepted in the room, or procurement released before the engineer of record has confirmed the whole load path. The control is a written change process for structural substitutions, with no order placed until the engineer of record's written confirmation is in hand, and the peer reviewer's comments resolved.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "same strength, cheaper and faster" and agrees. A transfer is never only a beam; it is connections above and below, services through it, fire rating and deflection under the floors it carries. Ask what else the change touches.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the owner's decision log: every significant decision recorded with its date, its basis and who made it. A structural substitution is exactly the kind of decision that log exists for. If a question arises years later, the log should show that the engineer of record confirmed the load path before anything was built.

Recap

Set the decision rule at the start, refuse to let procurement run ahead of approval, never treat a contractor's stamp or an engineer's silence as confirmation, keep out of technical disagreements, stay silent when the engineer raises the real issue, and decide in writing.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 103 review of structure.
checklist: I state the decision rule at the start: we decide in writing after review.
No procurement is released before the engineer of record confirms in writing.
I ask for the latest confirmation date when a supplier slot is at stake.
I never treat an engineer's silence as approval.
I ask the engineers to put disagreements in writing and resolve them.
I ask what else a substitution touches: connections, services, fire, deflection.
I record the decision and its basis in the owner's decision log.
I schedule structural decisions for my best hours where I can.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a contractor offers a cheaper transfer detail, I do not decide in the room. I open by saying the saving matters, and that we will decide in writing after the engineer of record and the peer reviewer have checked the load path and everything else the transfer touches: connections above and below, services, fire rating and deflection. When the contractor asks to release the order today, I hear the real question, whether commitment will run ahead of approval, and I turn it into a date: tell me the latest day we can confirm, and if the engineers cannot respond by then, we keep the original design. I never treat an engineer's silence as approval, never accept a specialty stamp as a whole-structure check, and never take sides between engineers in the room. I stay silent when the engineer raises the real issue, and I record the decision in the log.
terms: Value engineering — a review that proposes changes to reduce cost or time while keeping the required function, which must be checked before it is accepted.
Substitution — a proposal to replace a specified product, system or detail with a different one.
Post-tensioning — a method of strengthening concrete by tensioning steel tendons after the concrete has hardened.

hostile.q: The precast slot closes Friday. If you will not release the order, the two weeks we saved become four weeks lost. Why are you choosing delay?
hostile.a: I am not choosing delay; I am choosing not to commit to a structure that has not been checked. If the engineer of record can confirm by Friday, we will release. If not, we stay on the original design, which carries no slot risk and is already in your schedule. The saving is attractive, and if the review shows it works, I will want it on the next project too.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 103 Review: Load Paths, Transfers and Who Checks What
summary: Six questions test the week: gravity and lateral systems, the load path, what structural choices do to cost, the code's chain of documents and inspections, the load takedown and the substitution meeting. A Red Pen drill marks up a hypothetical structural change memo, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one idea: every load needs a continuous, checked path to the ground, and the owner's job is to make sure no decision, early in design or late in construction, breaks that path without the right engineer confirming it in writing.

Recall

Q. What is value engineering, and what must happen before it is accepted?

A. A review proposing changes that reduce cost or time while keeping the required function. The change must be checked by the engineer of record, and a peer reviewer where engaged, before it is accepted.

Q. What does an egress plan have to prove for a person who uses a wheelchair?

A. That there is an accessible route to accessible exits or areas of refuge, with communication, so the person can reach safety or wait for assistance.

Q. In concept, why does a company owner need a personal tax plan as well as a corporate one?

A. Because company decisions about salary, dividends and retained earnings drive the owner's personal tax and savings, so the two must be planned together with a licensed adviser.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, structure is where an owner's early choices and late approvals have the longest consequences. You will choose the grid and the uses, and you will approve the changes. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between a gravity system and a lateral force-resisting system?

Answer: The gravity system carries vertical loads from slabs to beams, columns or walls, and foundations. The lateral system, such as shear walls or braced or moment frames, carries wind and earthquake loads to the ground.

Question 2. What is a load path, and where do failures cluster?

Answer: The continuous chain of elements and connections that carries a load to the foundation. Failures and overruns cluster where a load changes direction: connections and transfers.

Question 3. Name the three places a structural decision moves money.

Answer: The frame itself, everything that grows with height such as exterior wall and risers, and efficiency, the units or parking gained or lost.

Question 4. What is a statement of special inspections, and who should engage the inspector?

Answer: The permit document listing what critical work will be specially inspected, how often and by whom. The owner usually engages the agency directly, so the inspector is independent of the contractor.

Question 5. How do you do a rough gravity load takedown?

Answer: Tributary area times dead and live load per floor, factored by the governing combination, added floor by floor, with units written beside every number and the real loads taken from the adopted ASCE 7.

Question 6. What is Rule 103?

Answer: Never let a structural member or connection change after design without the engineer of record confirming in writing that the whole load path still works; a shop drawing stamp is not that confirmation.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Bram taught load paths, gravity and lateral systems, transfers and floor-to-floor height. Ford took the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse of 1981, where a change from one rod to two doubled the load on a weak connection, giving Rule 103. Sage priced structural choices on the whole building. Ivo set out the code's chain of documents and inspections and compared Canada and Guyana. Bram ran a load takedown and the substitution meeting.

Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical structural change memo from a contractor. Find the defects before reading on.

Memo: Structural Substitution No. 4. We propose to replace the cast-in-place transfer beams at Level 2 with precast post-tensioned beams designed by our specialty engineer, saving 400,000 dollars and two weeks. The specialty engineer has stamped the design. The engineer of record has reviewed the shop drawings and returned them "No Exceptions Taken". Special inspections for the precast connections will be provided by our quality team. We will also relocate the rooftop water tank to the east bay for better access; no structural change required. Please confirm by return so we can release the precast order.

The defects. First, the memo treats the engineer of record's shop drawing review as confirmation of the load path. A shop drawing return stamp is not a written confirmation that the whole structure still works, which is Rule 103. Second, the specialty engineer's stamp covers his own elements, not their connection to the columns above and below or their effect on the rest of the building. Third, there is no peer reviewer comment, though a transfer level is exactly where one is warranted. Fourth, special inspections by the contractor's own quality team are not independent; the owner's special inspection agency should inspect the connections. Fifth, moving a rooftop water tank, which can weigh hundreds of kips, is called "no structural change", which is a takedown question for the engineer of record. Sixth, the memo asks for confirmation by return so the order can be released, putting commitment ahead of approval. Seventh, it says nothing about services through the beams, fire rating or deflection.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to a board deciding whether to accept a structural substitution. Time yourself, then read the model answer.

Model answer: "Every load in our building has to travel a continuous path to the ground, and most failures and overruns happen where that path changes direction, at connections and transfers. Our transfer level above the parking is the most critical structure we have. The contractor proposes a cheaper precast scheme. The saving is real, but we will not decide on cost or on a shop drawing stamp. The engineer of record will confirm in writing that the load path, the connections above and below, the services, the fire rating and the deflection all still work, and our independent peer reviewer will comment. Our own special inspection agency, not the contractor's team, will inspect the connections. No precast is ordered until that is done. The rooftop tank relocation is a separate load question and also goes to the engineer. Our rule is simple: no structural change without the engineer of record's written confirmation."

Scoring your drill

Record it on your phone and score it from 1 to 5 for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. For the hard question, imagine a board member saying: "We are paying a peer reviewer and an engineer of record. Isn't that paying twice?" A strong answer: "We are paying once for the design and once for an independent check of the decisions that cannot be undone. The cost is small against the structure, and it is the check that was missing in the Hyatt Regency collapse."

Three confusions to clear up

First, a sealed calculation from a specialty engineer is not the same as the engineer of record's confirmation; each engineer answers for a different scope. Second, a building department inspection is not a special inspection; the first is a regulatory check, the second is a detailed verification of critical work by an independent inspector. Third, a cheaper frame is not a cheaper building; height, envelope, services and efficiency can move more money than the frame itself.

One more habit for the week. Next time you walk any building, look up at one connection, a beam onto a column, a hanger or a balcony bracket, and trace where its load goes next. Ten seconds of tracing a real load path builds the instinct this week is about.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught that independent reviews, peer review, the lender's monitor and quantity surveyor audits, are only as useful as their independence and their scope. A structural peer review chosen by the engineer it checks, or scoped to exclude the transfer, is a review in name only.

What is a load path, and where do failures cluster?
Name the three places a structural decision moves money.

How do you do a rough gravity load takedown?
What is Rule 103?
head: The six questions
speak: Every load in a building needs a continuous path to the ground. The gravity system carries vertical loads and the lateral system carries wind and earthquake. Failures and overruns cluster where loads change direction: connections and transfers. A structural decision moves money in three places: the frame, everything that grows with height, and the units or parking gained or lost, so I compare options on the whole building. The code adopts ASCE 7 for loads and material standards for design, a licensed engineer of record seals it, and special inspectors I engage myself verify the critical work. A rough takedown is tributary area times factored load, floor by floor, with units on every number. Rule 103: never let a structural member or connection change after design without the engineer of record confirming in writing that the whole load path still works. A shop drawing stamp is not that confirmation.
terms: No Exceptions Taken — a common shop drawing review stamp meaning the reviewer found nothing to correct in general conformance, which is not a fresh design check.
Deflection — how far a structural member bends under load, which affects finishes, partitions and floors above.
Structural responsibility matrix — a list of every structural element with its designer, sealing engineer, inspector and governing standard.

hostile.q: Your engineer of record returned the precast shop drawings 'No Exceptions Taken'. Why do you need anything more before ordering?
hostile.a: Because that stamp confirms general conformance of what was submitted, not that the substitution works with the rest of the building. Before any order, I need the engineer of record's written confirmation that the load path, the connections into the columns above and below, the services through the beams, the fire rating and the deflection all still work, plus the peer reviewer's comments. That is our rule for every structural change, and it is the step that was missing in the best-known walkway collapse in American history.
